Chapter 9: Quantum Chromodynamics

9 Quantum Chromodynamics

9.1 Non Abelian Gauge Theories

  • Non Abelian gauge theories are the fundamentals of QCD (in fact, they ARE Quantum Chromodynamics).

    • We need to establish quite a bit more formal background in order to do actual physics, otherwise nothing would make sense

9.1.1 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras

Definition 9.1.1.1 (Non Abelian Gauge Group).

  • Suppose that you have a representation of a Lie Group, written as

    𝑅(𝐺)=𝑈=exp(𝑖𝜃𝑎𝑇𝑎)

  • 𝜃𝑎 is a number

  • 𝑇𝑎 are the group generators for the Lie Algebra that generates the Lie Group 𝐺.

  • The generators 𝑇𝑎 satisfy the commutation

    [𝑇𝑎,𝑇𝑏]=𝑖𝑓𝑎𝑏𝑐𝑇𝑐

  • If 𝑓𝑎𝑏𝑐=0, the gauge group 𝐺 is abelian

  • If 𝑓𝑎𝑏𝑐≠0, the gauge group 𝐺 is non abelian

  • The commutation relations […] are a mapping 𝒢︀×𝒢︀→𝒢︀, without having to have a well-defined product

    • In the special case that a product is well defined, [𝐴,𝐵]=𝐴𝐵−𝐵𝐴

  • Note: The Jacobi Identity must be satisfied regardless of the product being well defined

    • [𝐴,[𝐵,𝐶]]+[𝐵,[𝐶,𝐴]]+[𝐶,[𝐴,𝐵]]=0

    • By the Jacobi Identity,

      𝑓𝑎𝑏𝑑𝑓𝑑𝑐𝑒+𝑓𝑏𝑐𝑑𝑓𝑑𝑎𝑒+𝑓𝑐𝑎𝑑𝑓𝑑𝑏𝑒=0

Definition 9.1.1.2 (Ideal).

  • An ideal subalgebra ℑ⊂𝔤 is one that satisfies [𝑠,𝑖]∈ℑ∀𝑔∈𝔤,𝑖∈ℑ

Definition 9.1.1.3 (Simple).

  • A simple Lie Algebra 𝔤 is one that has no trivial ideal subalgebras

Example 9.1.1.4 (Simple Lie Algebras).

  • Very common Simple Lie Groups/Algebras are 𝔰𝔬(𝑁) and 𝔰𝔲(𝑁)
  • There is also the simplectic group 𝔰𝔭(𝑁)
  • All of these you will soon see

Definition 9.1.1.5 (Semisimple).

  • A semisimple Lie algebra 𝔤 is one that can be expressed as the direct sum of simple Lie Algebras 𝔤1,𝔤2,…,𝔤𝔫

    • That is,

      𝔤=𝔤1⊕𝔤2⊕𝔤3⊕…⊕𝔤𝔫

  • The standard model is a very common example of a Semisimple Lie Group

    • The Lie group for the Standard model is

      𝐺SM=SU(3)⊗SU(2)⊗𝑈(1)

    • The Lie algebra for the Standard model is

      𝔤SM=𝔰𝔲(3)⊕𝔰𝔲(2)⊕𝔲(1)

Theorem 9.1.1.6 (Hermicity).

  • All finite dimensional representations of semisimple Lie algebras are hermitian

Proof Hermicity.

  • Unfortunately I have tried and failed to prove it, so at this point i cannot provide a proof

⁠□

Definition 9.1.1.7 (Unitary Groups).

  • A unitary group is a group who’s representation satisfies

    ⟨𝜓⃗|𝜒⃗⟩=⟨𝜓⃗|𝑈†𝑈|𝜒⃗⟩
    • i.e. the inner product is conserved
  • This directly implies that 𝑈†𝑈=𝟙

  • Elements of SU(𝑁) have determinant 1

    • In general, matrix representations of unitary groups always have determinant 1 due to their being unitary

  • The group SU(𝑁) is defined by its action upon 𝑁 dimensional vector spaces

    • 𝑈=exp(𝑖𝜃𝑎𝑇𝑎)
      • In SU(𝑁), 𝑇𝑎 are always hermitian

    • There are 𝑁2−1 generators for SU(𝑁)

      • This implies that the dimension 𝑑(𝐺) is equal to 𝑑(𝐺)=𝑁2−1

Definition 9.1.1.8 (Orthogonal Group).

  • Orthogonal groups preserve a strictly real inner product

  • 𝑉⋅𝑊=𝑉⋅𝑂𝑇⋅𝑂⋅𝑊

  • This directly implies that 𝑂𝑇𝑂=𝟙

  • The dimension of an orthogonal group SO(𝑁) is 𝑑(SO(𝑁))=12𝑑(SU(𝑁))=12𝑁(𝑁−1)

    • This is due to the fact that there are half as many generators for orthogonal groups due to their strict realness

  • All elements of an orthogonal group (not special orthog.) have determinant det(𝑂)=±1

    • In SO(𝑁), the matrices are the ones with det(𝑂)=+1
    • This has no impact on the dimension of the group

Definition 9.1.1.9 (Simplectic Group).

  • Symplectic groups Sp(𝑁) are defined via preserving a quaternionic inner product

  • They satisfy

    Ω𝑆=−𝑆𝑇Ω

    where 𝑆∈Sp(𝑁) and

    Ω=(0𝕀−𝕀0)

  • There are, finally, the exceptional simple groups 𝐺2,𝐹4,𝐸6,𝐸7,𝐸8 which are of no use to standard model particle physics

  • The Only finite dimensional simple Lie Algebras are the algebras for the exceptional simple groups and 𝔰𝔬(𝑁),𝔰𝔲(𝑁),𝔰𝔭(𝑁)

9.1.2 Representations

  • Consider representations of SU(𝑁) groups

  • Free theories of 𝑁 fields are invariant under U(1)×SU(𝑁)

    • Since SU(𝑁) is simply connected, any representation of SU(𝑁) is one to one representation of exp(𝔰𝔲(𝑁))

Example 9.1.2.1 (Two Fields).

  • Consider 2 fields 𝜙1,𝜙2 with a kinetic lagrangian
ℒ︀𝑘𝑖𝑛=(𝜕𝜇𝜙1*)(𝜕𝜇𝜙1)+(𝜕𝜇𝜙2*)(𝜕𝜇𝜙2)=(𝜕𝜇𝜙⃗)†(𝜕𝜇𝜙⃗)

  • We can write

    𝜙⃗=(𝜙1𝜙2)
    • This is invariant under a global SU(2) symmetry 𝜙⃗→𝑈𝜙⃗

  • Generally, as we have seen, we can write

    𝑈=exp[𝑖(𝛼1𝜏1+𝛼2𝜏2+𝛼3𝜏3)]=exp(𝑖𝑎𝑎𝜏𝑎)𝑤/𝜏𝑎=1/2𝜎𝑎

  • Such 𝜏𝑎 satisfy

    𝜏𝑎:[𝜏𝑎,𝜏𝑏]=𝑖𝜖𝑎𝑏𝑐𝜏𝑐
  • This provides 𝑓𝑎𝑏𝑐=𝜀𝑎𝑏𝑐

Definition 9.1.2.2 (Fundamental).

  • A fundamental representation is the smallest non trivial representation of a Lie Algebra

  • For SU(𝑁), the fundamental representation is the set of 𝑁×𝑁 hermitian matricians with determinant 1

  • Under the fundamental representation, a set of 𝑁 fields transform (infinitesimally) as

    𝜙𝑖→𝜙𝑖+𝑖𝛼𝑎(𝑇fund𝑎)𝑖𝑗𝜙𝑗

    for some 𝛼𝑎∈ℝ

Definition 9.1.2.3 (Anti-fundamental Representation).

  • 𝑇anti-fund𝑎=−(𝑇fund𝑎)*
  • The anti-fund representation of a group is the conjugate of the fundamental representation
  • Notice that there is a minus sign in order to preserve the law [𝑇𝑎,𝑇𝑏]=𝑖𝑓𝑎𝑏𝑐𝑇𝑐

  • Therefore, the infinitesimal transformation law for anti-fundamental is

    𝜙𝑖*→𝜙𝑖*+𝑖𝛼𝑎(𝑇anti-fund𝑎)𝑖𝑗𝜙𝑗*=𝜙𝑖*−𝑖𝛼𝑎𝜙𝑗*(𝑇fund𝑎)𝑗𝑖

  • In order to determine the generators for a theory, we expand around 𝟙

    • In SU(2), the generators are 𝜎𝜇
    𝑇𝑎=𝜏𝑎≡𝜎𝑎2
    • In SU(3), the generators are eight (not 3⊗3‾=9) gellmann matrices (such that 𝑇𝑎=𝜆𝑎2) which are as follows:

  • Normalization of 𝑓𝑎𝑏𝑐 is arbitrary in QCD/non abelian gauge theory.

  • A commonly used convention for normalization (in physics) is

    ∑𝑐,𝑑𝑓𝑎𝑐𝑑𝑓𝑏𝑐𝑑=𝑁𝛿𝑎𝑏

    • In math, the convention is

      ∑𝑐,𝑑𝑓𝑎𝑐𝑑𝑓𝑏𝑐𝑑=𝛿𝑎𝑏

  • The fixing the normalization of structure constants implies that the normalization of generators is fixed in all representations

  • For representations,

    [𝑇𝑎,𝑇𝑏]=𝑖𝑓𝑎𝑏𝑐𝑇𝑐

    must hold when 𝑓𝑎𝑏𝑐 is the same

    • Notice that this equation is not invariant under a rescaling of 𝑇𝑅𝑐

  • Normalization of SU(𝑁):

    • It is normalized s.t.

      tr(𝑇𝑎𝑇𝑏)=12𝛿𝑎𝑏

  • In a general lie algebra, [𝑇𝑎,𝑇𝑏] is well defined and 𝑇𝑎𝑇𝐵 is not (as seen before)

    • In the fundamental representation of SU(𝑁), such generators, in fact, can be multiplied
    • 𝑇𝑎𝑇𝑏=12𝑁𝛿𝑎𝑏+12𝑑𝑎𝑏𝑐𝑇𝑐+12𝑖𝑓𝑎𝑏𝑐𝑇𝑐
    • 𝑑𝑎𝑏𝑐=2tr[𝑇𝑎{𝑇𝑏,𝑇𝑐}]

  • In SU(𝑁), there is a unique 𝑑𝑎𝑏𝑐 up to a constant

    • In SU(2), 𝑑𝑎𝑏𝑐=0

  • Some useful trace identities for generators are the following:

    tr[𝑇𝑎𝑇𝑏𝑇𝑐]=14(𝑑𝑎𝑏𝑐+𝑖𝑓𝑎𝑏𝑐)tr[𝑇𝑎𝑇𝑏𝑇𝑐𝑇𝑑]=14𝑁𝛿𝑎𝑏+18(𝑑𝑎𝑏𝑒+𝑖𝑓𝑎𝑏𝑒)×(𝑑𝑐𝑑𝑒+𝑖𝑓𝑐𝑑𝑒)

Definition 9.1.2.4 (Adjoint Representation).

  • The adjoint representation is the group acting upon its own elements

  • Extremely formally

    Ad:𝐺→GL(𝔤)
    with 𝐺 an element of a Lie group, 𝔤 an element of a Lie algebra, and GL being the group of invertible matrices
  • If the lie group generated by a lie algebra is 𝑒𝑋, then Ad𝐴(𝑋)=𝐴𝑋𝐴−1 with 𝐴∈𝐺.
  • The adjoint representation amounts to acting upon the space that is spanned by the generators, as you have seen
  • In SU(𝑁), there are 𝑁2−1 generators and hence there are 𝑁2−1 dimensions for the adjoint representation

  • Matrices in the adjoint representation are given by (𝑇adj𝑎)𝑏𝑐=−𝑖𝑓𝑎𝑏𝑐

    • For SU(2), the matrices are

      𝑇𝑎𝑑𝑗1=(00000−𝑖0𝑖0),𝑇𝑎𝑑𝑗2=(00𝑖000−𝑖00),𝑇𝑎𝑑𝑗3=(0−𝑖0𝑖00000)
  • In SU(3), they are 8×8 matrices as you may be able to guess
  • Gauge fields transform in the adjoint representation

Definition 9.1.2.5 (Casimirs).

  • Casimirs are used to “characterize representations” [1]

Definition 9.1.2.6 (Quadratic Casimir).

  • The Quadratic Casimir is defined via

    (∑𝑎)𝑇𝑅𝑎𝑇𝑅𝑎=𝐶2(𝑅)𝟙

Theorem 9.1.2.7 (Schur's Lemma).

  • Group elements that commute with all other elements are proportional to 𝟙

  • This theorem is extremely nontrivial. You can see a proof in [2]

  • I am, however, able to provide a proof on why the 𝑇𝑎𝑇𝑎 commutes with everything

    [𝑇𝑅𝑎𝑇𝑅𝑎,𝑇𝑅𝑏]=(𝑖𝑓𝑎𝑏𝑐𝑇𝑅𝑐)𝑇𝑅𝑎+𝑇𝑅𝑎(𝑖𝑓𝑎𝑏𝑐𝑇𝑅𝑐)=−𝑖𝑓𝑎𝑏𝑐{𝑇𝑅𝑐,𝑇𝑅𝑎}=0

  • Evaluating quadratic Casimirs involve choosing generators such that

    𝑓𝑟[𝑇𝑝𝑎,𝑇𝑝𝑏]=𝑇(𝑅)𝑎𝑏
    • 𝑇(𝑅) is known as the index

  • In the fundamental representation, the convention implies that

    • 𝑇(fund)≡𝑇𝐹=12 since (T^a(i j) T^b(i j) = 1.2 delta^(a b))

  • In the adjoint representation, 𝑇(adj)≡𝑇𝐴=𝑁

    • This is due to the fact that 𝑓𝑎𝑐𝑑𝑓𝑏𝑐𝑑=𝑁𝛿𝑎𝑏

  • Setting 𝑎=𝑏 and summing over 𝑎 for the definition of 𝑇(𝑅) yields

    • 𝑑(𝑅)𝐶2(𝑅)=𝑇(𝑅)𝑑(𝐺)
      • 𝑑(𝑅) is the dimension of the representation
      • 𝑑(𝐺) is the dimension of the group

  • Fundamental Casimir:

    • 𝐶𝐹=𝐶2(𝑓𝑢𝑛𝑑)=𝑁2−12𝑁
    • In SU(2), 𝐶𝐹=34
    • In SU(3), 𝐶𝐹=43

  • Adjoint Casimir:

    • 𝐶𝐴≡𝐶2(adj)=𝑁
    • Generally, terms in YM theories will contain at least some factors of 𝐶𝐹 and 𝐶𝐴

  • For any representation,

    tr([𝑇𝑅𝑎,𝑇𝑅𝑏]𝑇𝑅𝑐)=𝑖𝑓𝑎𝑏𝑐tr(𝑇𝑅𝑑𝑇𝑅𝑑)=𝑖𝑓𝑎𝑏𝑐𝑇(𝑅)

    • This implies that

      𝑓𝑎𝑏𝑐=−𝑖𝑇𝐹tr([𝑡𝑎,𝑡𝑏]𝑡𝑐)

  • In SU(𝑁), the Fierz Identity is satisfied:

    • ∑𝑎𝑇𝑖𝑗𝑎𝑇𝑘𝑙𝑎=12(𝛿𝑖𝑙𝛿𝑗𝑘−1𝑁𝛿𝑖𝑗𝛿𝑘𝑙)
    • Since generators in SU(𝑁) are traceless, the sum over 𝛿𝑖𝑗 and 𝛿𝑘𝑙 yields zero

    • Hence,

      tr[𝑇𝑎𝐴]tr[𝑇𝑎𝐵]=12[tr(𝐴𝐵)−1𝑁tr(𝐴)tr(𝐵)]

Definition 9.1.2.8 (Anomaly Coefficient).

  • An anomaly coefficient 𝐴(𝑅) is defined by the equation

    tr[𝑇𝑎{𝑇𝑏,𝑇𝑐}]=12𝐴(𝑅)𝑑𝑎𝑏𝑐=𝐴(𝑅)tr[𝑇𝑎{𝑇𝑏,𝑇𝑐}]

9.2 Wilson Lines

9.2.1 Abelian Wilson Lines

  • The motivation between wilson lines is a want for telling if 𝜙(𝑥)=𝜙(𝑦) (some how)

  • Notice that one cannot simply take the difference since

    𝜙(𝑥)−𝜙(𝑦)→𝑒𝑖𝛼(𝑥)𝜙(𝑥)−𝑒𝑖𝛼(𝑦)𝜙(𝑦)
    • It is additionally impossible to take any notion of 𝜕𝜇𝜙 due to derivative definition based on differences

Definition 9.2.1.1 (Wilson Line).

  • A wilson line 𝑊(𝑥,𝑦) is something that transforms as 𝑊(𝑥,𝑦)→𝑒𝑖𝛼(𝑥)𝑊(𝑥,𝑦)𝑒−𝑖𝛼(𝑦)

    • This is a “bi-local transformation” [1]

  • A key feature of Wilson lines is that they satisfy the property

    𝑊(𝑥,𝑦)𝜙(𝑦)−𝜙(𝑥)→𝑒𝑖𝛼(𝑥)𝑊(𝑥,𝑦)𝑒−𝑖𝛼(𝑦)𝑒𝑖𝛼(𝑦)𝜙(𝑦)−𝑒𝑖𝛼(𝑥)𝜙(𝑥)=𝑒𝑖𝛼(𝑥)(𝑊(𝑥,𝑦)𝜙(𝑦)−𝜙(𝑥))

  • Taking 𝑦𝜇=𝑥𝜇+𝛿𝑥𝜇, we can obtain the derivative via

    𝐷𝜇𝜙(𝑥)≡lim𝛿𝑥𝜇→0𝑊(𝑥,𝑥+𝛿𝑥)𝜙(𝑥+𝛿𝑥)−𝜙(𝑥)𝛿𝑥

    • This gives a transformation law that we expect

      𝐷𝜇𝜙(𝑥)⟶𝑒𝑖𝛼(𝑥)𝐷𝜇𝜙(𝑥)

  • Writing the wilson line in terms of a perturbation,

    𝑊(𝑥,𝑥+𝛿𝑥)=1−𝑒𝛿𝑥𝜇𝐴𝜇(𝑥)+𝒪︀(𝛿𝑥2)

    • This gives, as we expect, the abelian gauge transformation

      𝐴𝜇(𝑥)→𝐴𝜇(𝑥)+1𝑒𝜕𝜇𝛼(𝑥)
    • The Guage field is a connection

  • This provides the abelian covariant derivative

    𝐷𝜇𝜙(𝑥)=𝜕𝜇𝜙(𝑥)−𝑖𝑒𝐴𝜇𝜙

  • The closed-form for the wilson line is written as

    𝑊𝑃(𝑥,𝑦)=exp(𝑖𝑒∫𝑦𝑥𝐴𝜇(𝑧)𝑑𝑧𝜇)
    • Notice that this is a line integral
    • This is the true Wilson Line

  • Parametrizing the wilson line with 𝑧𝜇(𝜆) such that 0≤𝜆≤1 and 𝑧𝜇(0)=𝑦𝜇,𝑧𝜇(1)=𝑥𝜇, we obtain that

    𝑊𝑃(𝑥,𝑦)=exp(𝑖𝑒∫01𝑑𝑧𝜇(𝜆)𝑑𝜆𝐴𝜇(𝑧(𝜆))𝑑𝜆)

  • We can test how this behaves under a gauge transformation

    • 𝑊𝑃(𝑥,𝑦)→exp[𝑖𝑒∫𝑦𝑥𝐴𝜇(𝑧)𝑑𝑧𝜇+𝑖∫𝑦𝑥𝜕𝜇𝛼(𝑧)𝑑𝑧𝜇]=𝑒𝑖𝛼(𝑥)𝑊𝑃(𝑥,𝑦)𝑒−𝑖𝛼(𝑦)
    • This behaves correctly from our definition of a Wilson line

  • Wilson Loops:

    • Setting 𝑥=𝑦, we obtain that

      𝑊𝑃loop=exp(𝑖𝑒∮𝑃𝐴𝜇𝑑𝑥𝜇)

  • Via stokes’ theorem,

    𝑊𝑝𝑙𝑜𝑜𝑝=exp(𝑖𝑒2∫Σ𝐹𝜇𝜈𝑑𝜎𝜇𝜈)=1+𝑖𝑒2∫Σ𝐹𝜇𝜈𝑑𝜎𝜇𝜈+𝒪︀(𝑒2)

    where 𝜎𝜇𝜈 is a surface element

  • Notice that now the wilson line only depends on the field tensor 𝐹𝜇𝜈 (this should not be surprising since it depends on the gauge field)

  • Checking the transformation for the commutator [𝐷𝜇,𝐷𝜈], we obtain

    [𝐷𝜇,𝐷𝜈]𝜙(𝑥)→𝑒𝑖𝛼(𝑥)[𝐷𝜇,𝐷𝜈]𝜙(𝑥)

    • therefore, we obtain

      [𝐷𝜇,𝐷𝜈]𝜙(𝑥)=([𝜕𝜇,𝜕𝜈]−𝑖𝑒[𝜕𝜇,𝐴𝜈]+𝑖𝑒[𝜕𝜈,𝐴𝜇])𝜙(𝑥)=−𝑖𝑒𝐹𝜇𝜈(𝑥)

    • Hence, we can define the EM field tensor as

      𝐹𝜇𝜈(𝑥)=𝑖𝑒[𝐷𝜇,𝐷𝜈]

9.2.2 Non Abelian Wilson Lines

  • We would like to repeat the same process as we did with abelian wilson lines

    • Lagrangians have more symmetry than just phase rotation in non abelian theories (by definition)

  • Consider the kinetic lagrangian with 𝑁 particles

    ℒ︀𝑘𝑖𝑛=∑𝑗=1𝑛𝜓̄𝑗(𝑖𝜕−𝑚)𝜓𝑗
    • This has a global SU(𝑁) symmetry

  • Such particles transform as

    𝜓𝑖→(𝑒𝑖𝛼𝑎𝑇𝑎)𝑖𝑗𝜓𝑗
    • 𝛼𝑎 is not a function of 𝑥 for global symmetries

Definition 9.2.2.1 (Non Abelian Wilson Line).

  • We are now motivated to write

    𝑊𝑃(𝑥,𝑦)=𝑃{exp(𝑖𝑔∫𝑦𝑥𝐴𝜇𝑎(𝑧)𝑇𝑎𝑑𝑧𝜇)}
    where 𝑃 is path ordering

  • The Taylor expansion of the wilson line is

    𝑊𝑃(𝑧,𝑦)=1+𝑖𝑔∫01𝑑𝑧𝜇(𝜆)𝑑𝜆𝐴𝜇𝑎(𝑧(𝜆))𝑇𝑎𝑑𝜆−12𝑔2∫01𝑑𝜆∫01𝑑𝜏𝑑𝑧𝜇(𝜆)𝑑𝜆𝑑𝑧𝜈(𝜏)𝑑𝜏𝐴𝜇𝑎(𝑧(𝜆))𝐴𝜈𝑏(𝑧(𝜏))(𝑇𝑎𝑇𝑏𝜃(𝜆−𝜏)+𝑇𝑏𝑇𝑎𝜃(𝜏−𝜆))+…

  • Under a gauge transformation

    𝑊𝑃(𝑥,𝑦)=𝑒𝑖𝛼𝑎(𝑥)𝑇𝑎𝑊𝑃(𝑥,𝑦)𝑒−𝑖𝛼𝑎(𝑦)𝑇𝑎

    which definitely looks correct

  • We are motivated to define a variable 𝐴𝜇≡𝐴𝜇𝑎𝑇𝑎

    • This gives

      𝑊𝑃(𝑥,𝑦)=𝑃{exp(𝑖𝑔∫𝑦−𝑥𝑥𝐴𝜇(𝑧)𝑑𝑧𝜇)}

  • An infinitesimal transformation for 𝑊 is

    𝑊(𝑥𝜇,𝑥𝜇+𝛿𝑥𝜇)=1+𝑖𝜖𝐴𝜇𝛿𝑥𝜇

  • Local transformations can be expressed in terms of

    𝑈(𝑥)=𝑒𝑖𝛼𝑎(𝑥)𝑇𝑎
    • In SU(𝑁), 𝑈†(𝑦)=𝑈(𝑦)

  • Then,

    𝜓⃗=𝑈(𝑥)·𝜓⃗(𝑥)𝑊(𝑥,𝑦)→𝑈(𝑥)𝑊(𝑥,𝑦)𝑈†(𝑦)

  • We would like to analyze what happens to the gauge field under such a transformation

    • Consider how the covariant derivative transforms:

      𝐷𝜇𝐴⃗→𝑈·𝐷𝜇𝐴⃗

  • Therefore, we have that

    (𝜕𝜇−𝑖𝑔𝐴′𝜇)𝑈𝜓=𝑈(𝜕𝜇−𝑖𝑔𝐴𝜇)𝜓

    where 𝐴𝜇 is the transformed 𝐴𝜇

  • Therefore, the transformation for 𝐴𝜇𝑎 is

    𝐴𝜇𝑎(𝑥)→𝐴𝜇𝑎(𝑥)+1𝑔𝜕𝜇𝛼𝑎(𝑥)−𝑓𝑎𝑏𝑐𝛼𝑏(𝑥)𝐴𝜇𝑐+𝑂(𝛼2)

  • The covariant derivative commutator transforms as

    [𝐷𝜇,𝐷𝜈]𝜓(𝑥)=(−𝑖𝑔(𝜕𝜇𝐴𝜈−𝜕𝜈𝐴𝜇)−𝑔2[𝐴𝜇,𝐴𝜈])𝜓(𝑥)

    • This allwos for a definition of the gluon field tensor:

      𝐹𝜇𝜈≡𝑖𝑔[𝐷𝜇,𝐷𝜈]=(𝜕𝜇𝐴𝜈−𝜕𝜈𝐴𝜇)−𝑖𝑔[𝐴𝜇,𝐴𝜈]𝐹𝜇𝜈=𝐹𝜇𝜈𝑎𝑇𝑎

    -

    𝐹𝜇𝜈𝑎=𝜕𝜇𝐴𝜈𝑎−𝜕𝜈𝐴𝜇𝑎+𝑔𝑓𝑎𝑏𝑐𝐴𝜇𝑏𝐴𝜈𝑐

  • The transformation law for the field tensor is

    𝐹𝜇𝜈𝑎→𝐹𝜇𝜈𝑎−𝑓𝑎𝑏𝑐𝛼𝑏𝐹𝜇𝜈𝑐

    which is the same whether or not 𝛼 is global or local

    • This is because

      𝐹𝜇𝜈𝛼=−𝐹𝜈𝜇𝛼

  • Kinetic terms in the lagrangian only depend on 𝐹𝜇𝜈𝑎

    • The SU(𝑁) lagrangian is

      ℒ︀=−14(𝐹𝜇𝜈𝑎)2+∑𝑖,𝑗=1𝑁𝜓̄𝑖(𝑖𝛿𝑖𝑗𝜕+𝑔𝐴𝜇𝑎𝑇𝑖𝑗𝑎−𝑚𝛿𝑖𝑗)𝜓𝑗
    • In this lagrangian, 𝑔 acts as −𝑒

  • There is an extra term that is consistent with gauge invariance that can be added to this lagrangian:

ℒ︀𝜃=𝜃𝜀𝜇𝜈𝛼𝛽𝐹𝜇𝜈𝛼𝐹𝛼𝛽𝛼=2𝜃𝜕𝜇(𝜀𝜇𝜈𝛼𝛽𝐴𝜈𝛼𝐹𝛼𝛽𝛼)

  • Notice that this is a total derivative, hence it does not contribute perturbatively

  • There should be non perturbative effects that this term adds (the lack of them is known as the strong CP problem)

  • I claim that there is no conserved current for this lagrangian

  • Consider the expansion of the lagrangian

    ℒ︀=−14(𝜕𝜇𝐴𝜈𝑎−𝜕𝜈𝐴𝜇𝑎+𝑔𝑓𝑎𝑏𝑐𝐴𝜇𝑏𝐴𝜈𝑐)2+𝜓̄𝑖(𝑖𝛿𝑖𝑗𝛾𝜇𝜕𝜇+𝑔𝛾𝜇𝐴𝜇𝑎𝑇𝑖𝑗𝑎−𝑚𝛿𝑖𝑗)𝜓𝑗

    • The EoM for this lagrangian are

      𝜕𝜇𝐹𝜇𝜈𝑎+𝑔𝑓𝑎𝑏𝑐𝐴𝜇𝑏𝐹𝜇𝜈𝑐=−𝑔𝜓̄𝑖𝛾𝜈𝑇𝑖𝑗𝑎𝜓𝑗(Gauge)

      and

      −(𝑖𝜕−𝑚)𝜓𝑖=−𝑔𝐴𝑎𝑇𝑖𝑗𝑎𝜓𝑗(Ferm.)

  • The global symmetries for this are

    𝜓𝑖→𝜓𝑖+𝑖𝛼𝑎𝑇𝑖𝑗𝑎𝜓𝑗𝐴𝜇𝑎→𝐴𝜇𝑎−𝑓𝑎𝑏𝑐𝛼𝑏𝐴𝜇𝑐

    • By Noether’s theorem,

      𝐽𝜇=∑𝑛𝜕𝐿𝜕(𝜕𝜇𝜙𝑛)𝛿𝜙𝑛𝛿𝛼

  • In a non abelian theory, there are 𝑁2−1 currents

    • Summing ovr 𝜓𝑖 and 𝐴𝜇𝑎 provides

      𝐽𝑚𝜇=−𝜓̄𝑖𝛾𝜇𝑇𝑖𝑗𝑎𝜓𝑗+𝑓𝑎𝑏𝑐𝐴𝜈𝑏𝐹𝑐𝜇𝜈

  • Notice, however, that this current is gauge invariant.

    • Hence, it is not physical

  • We can try and create a matter current

    𝑗𝜇𝑎=−𝜓𝑖̄𝛾𝜇𝑇𝑖𝑗𝑎𝜓𝑗

    • This satisfies

      𝐷𝜇𝑗𝜇𝑎=0
    • It Still doesnt satisfy 𝜕𝜇𝑗𝜇𝑎=0

Theorem 9.2.2.2 (Weinberg Witten theorem).

  • A non abelian symmetry for massless spin 1 implies that there is no gauge invariant conserved charge

9.2.3 The Gluon Propagator

9.2.3.1 F-P ghosts

  • To Start, let us consider the equations of motion for a photon with an external current

    (𝑔𝜇𝜈☐−𝜕𝜇𝜕𝜈)𝐴𝑚=𝐽𝜈
    • This is not invertible, similar to the gluon equation of motion
    𝑓(𝜉)=∫𝒟︀𝜋𝑒−𝑖∫𝑑4𝑥12𝜉(𝐷𝜋)2=∫𝒟︀𝜋𝑒−𝑖∫𝑑4𝑥12𝜉(𝐷𝜋−𝜕𝜇𝐴𝜇)2
    • This is independed of 𝐴𝜇 since we can take 𝜋→𝜋−1□𝜕𝜇𝐴𝜇

  • Therefore, we obtained

    ∫𝒟︀𝐴𝜇𝒟︀𝜙𝑖𝑒𝑖∫𝑑4𝑥𝐿[𝐴,𝜙𝑖]=1𝑓(𝜉)∫𝒟︀𝜋𝒟︀𝐴𝜇𝒟︀𝜙𝑖𝑒𝑖∫𝑑4𝑥(𝐿(𝐴,𝜙𝑖)−12𝜉(𝜕𝜇𝐴𝜇)2)=[1𝑓(𝜉)∫𝒟︀𝜋]∫𝒟︀𝐴𝜇𝒟︀𝜙𝑖𝑒𝑖∫𝑑4𝑥(𝐿[𝐴,𝜙𝑖]−12𝜉(𝜕𝜇𝐴𝜇)2)

    in QED

  • We want to do a similar thing for ℚℂ𝔻

    • The gauge transformation is

      𝐴𝜇𝑎→𝐴𝜇𝑎+1𝑔𝜕𝜇𝛼𝑎+𝑓𝑎𝑏𝑐𝐴𝜇𝑏𝜋𝑐

  • Notice that there are 𝑁2−1 𝜋𝑎 fields due to them transforming in the adjoint represention

  • Since 𝜋𝑎 transforms in the adjoint rep we can write

    𝐴𝜇𝑎→𝐴𝜇𝑎+1𝑔𝐷𝜇𝜋𝑎

    where the adjoint covar. derivative is

    𝐷𝜇𝜋𝑎=𝜕𝜇𝜋𝑎+𝑔𝑓𝑎𝑏𝑐𝐴𝜇𝑏𝜋𝑐

  • We now have the machinery to write a functional

    𝑓[𝐴]=∫𝐷𝜋exp[−𝑖∫𝑑4𝑥12𝜉(𝜕𝜇𝐷𝜇𝜋𝑎)2]

“Tickle Tip”

  • Define 𝛼𝑎[𝐴] s.t.

    𝜕𝜇𝐴𝜇𝑎=1𝑔𝜕𝜇𝐷𝜇𝑎𝛼𝑎[𝐴]

  • Therefore,

    𝑓[𝐴]=∫𝒟︀𝜋exp[−𝑖∫𝑑4𝑥12𝜉(𝜕𝜇𝐴𝜈𝛼−𝜕𝜈𝐴𝜇𝛼)2]

  • This allows us to obtain the full path integral

    ∫𝐷𝐴𝐷𝜙𝑖𝑒𝑖∫𝑑4𝑥𝐿(𝐴,𝜙𝑖)=∫𝐷𝜋𝐷𝐴𝐷𝜙𝑖1𝑓[𝐴]exp(𝑖∫𝑑4𝑥𝐿(𝐴,𝜙𝑖)−12𝜉(𝜕𝜇𝐴𝜇−𝜕𝜇𝐴𝜇)2)=(∫𝒟︀𝜋)∫𝒟︀𝐴𝒟︀𝜙𝑖1𝑓[𝐴]exp(𝑖∫𝑑4𝑥𝐿(𝐴,𝜙𝑖)−12𝜉(𝜕𝜇𝐴𝜇)2)

  • We now wish to rewrite 𝑓[𝐴] (?)

    • 𝑓=1det(𝜕𝜇𝐷𝜇)2×const.

  • Then,

    𝑍[0]=const×∫𝒟︀𝐴𝑚𝒟︀𝜙𝑖(det(ℳ︀𝑚𝑛))×exp{𝑖∫𝑑4𝑥[ℒ︀(𝐴,𝜙𝑖)−12𝜉(𝜕𝜇𝐴𝑚𝑎)2]}

  • We can use identities for gaussians to write

    det(𝜕𝜇𝐷𝜇)=∫𝒟︀𝑐̄𝒟︀𝑐exp(𝑖∫𝑑4𝑥𝑐̄(−𝜕𝜇𝐷𝜇)𝑐)

    • The identity involved in this is

      det(𝒪︀)=∫𝒟︀𝜓̄𝒟︀𝜓exp(−𝑖∫𝜓̄𝒪︀𝜓)

  • Hence, we obtain the result that

    𝑍[𝑐]=const.×∫𝒟︀𝐴𝜇𝒟︀𝜙𝒟︀𝑐̄𝒟︀𝑐×exp{𝑖∫𝑑4𝑥[𝐿(𝐴,𝜙)−12𝜉(𝜕𝜇𝐴𝜇)2−𝑐̄𝑎𝜕𝜇𝐷𝜇𝑐𝑎]}

  • We have obtained a very bad result:

    • In QCD, as a result of trying to find a gluon propagator, we find these annoying things called Fadeev-Popov ghosts and antighosts

    • They pop up out of nowhere and are not gauge invariant

      • They are aphysical clearly

  • The Lagrangian must (and I mean must unless you are willing to work in a obnoxious gauge) be written with these in mind

ℒ︀𝑅𝜉=−14(𝐹𝜇𝜈𝑎)2−12𝜉(𝜕𝜇𝐴𝜇𝑎)2+(𝜕𝜇𝑐̄𝑎)(𝛿𝑎𝑐𝜕𝜇+𝑔𝑓𝑎𝑏𝑐𝐴𝜇𝑏)𝑐𝑐

  • This is called the Fadeev-Popov lagrangian

  • Luckily, we also have the gluon propagator

=𝑖−𝑔𝜇𝜈+(1−𝜉)𝑝𝜇𝑝𝜈𝑝2𝑝2+𝑖𝜀𝛿𝑎𝑏

  • Observe that

    1=∫𝒟︀𝜋𝛿(𝐺(𝐴𝜇𝑎−𝐷𝜇𝜋𝑎))det(𝛿𝐺[𝐴𝜇𝑎−𝐷𝜇𝜋𝑎]𝛿𝜋𝑎)

  • 𝐺[𝐴] is a functional which represents our choice of gauge

  • Then,

    det[𝛿𝐺{𝐴𝑚𝑎−𝐷𝑚𝜎𝑎}𝛿𝜎𝑏]=det(𝜕𝑚𝐷𝑚)=1𝑓[𝐴]=∫𝒟︀𝑐̄𝒟︀𝑐exp(𝑖∫𝑑4𝑥𝑐̄𝑎(−𝜕𝑚𝐷𝑚)𝑐𝑎)

  • Multiplying 𝑍[0] by 1 yields

    𝑍[0]=const×∫𝒟︀𝜋∫𝒟︀𝐴𝑚𝒟︀𝜙𝑖𝛿(𝐺[𝐴𝑚𝑎−𝐷𝑚𝜋𝑎])×det(𝛿𝐺[𝐴𝑚𝑎−𝐷𝑚𝜋𝑎]𝛿𝜋𝑏)exp(𝑖∫𝑑4𝑥ℒ︀[𝐴,𝜙])

  • We use the trick of shifting

    𝐴𝜇𝑎→𝐴𝜇𝑎+𝐷𝜇𝜋𝑎

    due to gauge invariance

  • Our result is that

    ⇒𝑍[0]=const.(∫𝐷𝜋)∫𝐷𝐴𝜇𝐷𝜙𝑖𝛿(𝐺[𝐴𝜇𝑎])×det(𝛿𝐺[𝐴𝜇𝑎−𝐷𝜇𝜋𝑎]𝛿𝛼𝑏)𝜋→0×exp(𝑖∫𝑑4𝑥𝐿[𝐴,𝜙𝑖])

  • Shifting 𝐺 by a constant keeps the determinant the same. Therefore, we can average over a gaussian which yields

∫𝒟︀𝜒exp(−𝑖∫𝑑4𝑥𝑋22𝜉)𝛿(𝐺[𝐴𝑚𝑎]−𝜒)=exp(−𝑖∫𝑑4𝑥12𝜉𝐺[𝐴𝑚𝑎]2)
  • This yields our final form of 𝑍[0]
𝑍[0]=const×∫𝒟︀𝐴𝜇𝒟︀𝜙𝑖det(𝛿𝐺[𝐴𝜇,𝜙𝑖]𝛿𝜙𝑗)×exp[𝑖∫𝑑4𝑥(𝐿[𝐴,𝜙𝑖]−12𝑔𝐺[𝐴𝜇]2)]
9.2.3.2 BRST Invariance

  • There is another symmetry that the lagrangian is invariant under.

    • This symmetry involves grassmann numbers and qcd ghosts

  • Consider the lagrangian

    ℒ︀=−14𝐹𝜇𝜈2+(𝐷𝜇𝜙𝑖*)(𝐷𝜇𝜙𝑖)−𝑚2𝜙𝑖*𝜙𝑖−12𝜉(𝜕𝜇𝐴𝜇)2−𝑐̄☐𝑐

  • If we define a shift

    𝜙𝑖(𝑥)→𝑒𝑖𝜃(𝑥)𝜙𝑖(𝑥)≈𝜙𝑖(𝑥)+𝑖𝜃(𝑥)𝜙𝑖(𝑥)𝐴𝜇(𝑥)→𝐴𝜇(𝑥)+1𝑒𝜕𝜇𝜃(𝑥)

    and either use the EOM or take

    (𝜕𝜇𝐴𝜇)2→(𝜕𝜇𝐴𝜇)2+2𝑒(𝜕𝜇𝐴𝜇)(𝜃□𝑐)+1𝑒2(𝜃□𝑐)(𝜃□𝑐)𝑐̄(𝑥)→𝑐̄(𝑥)−1𝑒𝜃1𝜉𝜕𝜇𝐴𝜇(𝑥)

    , this lagrangian is invariant

  • This gives us BRST Invariance

Definition 9.2.3.2.1 (BRST Invariance).

  • BRST Invariance is a generalization of guage invariance for the Fadeev Popov lagrangian

  • This works in the non-abelian case similarly, where the lagrangian is

    ℒ︀𝐹𝑃=ℒ︀[𝐴𝜇𝑎,𝜙𝑖]−12𝜉(𝜕𝜇𝐴𝜇𝑎)2+(𝜕𝜇𝑐̄𝑎)(𝐷𝜇𝑐𝑎)

  • One can define transformations

    𝜙𝑖→𝜙𝑖+𝑖𝜃𝑎𝑇𝑖𝑗𝑎𝜙𝑗𝐴𝜇𝑎→𝐴𝜇𝑎+1𝑔𝜃𝐷𝜇𝑐𝑎𝑐̄𝑎→𝑐̄𝑎−1𝑔𝜃1𝜉𝜕𝜇𝐴𝜇𝑎

    which leave everything but 𝐷𝜇 invariant. Hence. we need a final transformation which, after a lot of algebra, results in

𝐷𝜇𝑐𝑎→𝐷𝜇𝑐𝑎+𝜃𝑓𝑎𝑏𝑐(𝐷𝜇𝑐𝑏)𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑎→𝑐𝑎−12𝜃𝑓𝑎𝑏𝑐𝑐𝑏𝑐𝑐

  • or alternatively, after more algebra,

    𝐷𝜇𝑐𝑎→𝐷𝜇𝑐𝑎+𝑔𝑓𝑎𝑏𝑐(𝐷𝜇𝑐𝑏)𝑐𝑐−𝑔𝑓𝑎𝑏𝑐[12(𝜕𝜇𝑐𝑏)𝑐𝑐+12𝑐𝑏(𝜕𝜇𝑐𝑐)+𝑔2𝐴𝜇𝑏𝑓𝑐𝑑𝑒𝑐𝑑𝑐𝑒]
9.2.3.3 Axial gauges

Summary

  • Axial gauges are not very useful to work with but they remove the ghosts that are inconvenient to work with

  • The gluon propagator in an axial gauge is

    𝑖Πlightcone𝜇𝜈𝑎𝑏=𝑖𝑝2+𝑖𝜖[−𝑖𝑔𝜇𝜈+𝑟𝜇𝑝𝜈+𝑝𝜇𝑟𝜈𝑟𝑝]𝛿𝑎𝑏

    which, as you may be able to see, is not the most fun to work with

  • The most general lagrangian that we can write to gauge fix our other one is

    −12𝜆(𝜕𝜇𝐴𝜇𝑎)2+𝑐̄𝑎𝜕𝜇(𝛿𝑎𝑏𝜕𝜇+𝑔𝑓𝑎𝑏𝑐𝐴𝜇𝑏)𝑐𝑐

    with two parameters: 𝜆, a scalar, and 𝑟𝜇, a 4-vector.

  • The general propagator in this axial gauge is

    Π𝑎𝑥𝑖𝑎𝑙𝜇𝜈𝑎𝑏=𝑖𝑝2+𝑖𝜖[−𝑔𝜇𝜈+𝑟𝜇𝑝𝜈+𝑟𝜈𝑝𝜇𝑟·𝑝−(𝑟2+𝜆𝑝2)𝑝𝜇𝑝𝜈𝑝2]𝛿𝑎𝑏
    • We of course want this to satisfy the ward identity, but we do not have to change anything since it already does.

  • In the Lightcone gauge, we force that 𝑟2=0, 𝜆=0, which yields our propagator

9.3 Lattice QCD

Summary

  • Lattice QCD works by discretizing standard QCD into plaquettes and evaluating wilson loops on them
  • Fields are at specific lattice sites

Definition 9.3.1 (Discrete Wilson line).

  • First, lets consider some notation. 𝜇̂ and 𝜈̂ will be unit vectors (of length 𝑎 since in lattice qcd, everything is scaled by such a factor) in the 𝜇 and 𝜈 directions. 𝑊𝜇(𝑛) will denote a wilson line at some site 𝑛 and some other site 𝑛+𝜇̂

Evaluating Plaquettes:

  • How do we evaluate plaquettes?

    • Consider the Campbell Baker Hausdorff formula:

      exp(𝐴)exp(𝐵)=exp(𝐴+𝐵+12[𝐴,𝐵]+…)

  • Applying this to our definition of 𝑊𝜇𝜈,

    ln𝑊𝑚𝜈(𝑁)=𝑖𝑎(𝐴𝜇(𝑛)+𝐴𝜈(𝑛+𝜇̂)−𝐴𝜇(𝑛+𝜈̂)−𝐴𝜈(𝑛))+𝑎22{[𝐴𝜈(𝑁)+𝐴𝜇(𝑛+𝜈̂),𝐴𝜈(𝑛+𝜇̂)−𝐴𝜇(𝑛)]−[𝐴𝜈(𝑁),𝐴𝜇(𝑛+𝜈̂)]−[𝐴𝜈(𝑛+𝜇̂),𝐴𝜇(𝑛)]}+𝒪︀(𝑎3)

  • Via a taylor expansion,

    𝐴𝜈(𝑛+𝜇̂)=𝐴𝜈(𝑛)+𝑎𝜕𝜇𝐴𝜈(𝑛)+𝑂(𝑎2)

    ,

    𝑊𝜇𝜈(𝑛)=exp{𝑖𝑎2(𝜕𝜇𝐴𝜈(𝑛)−𝜕𝜈𝐴𝜇(𝑛))+𝑎2[𝐴𝜇(𝑛),𝐴𝜈(𝑛)]+𝑂(𝑎3)}=exp{𝑖𝑎2𝐹𝜇𝜈(𝑛)+𝑂(𝑎3)}

  • Consider the Yang Mills action:

    𝑆𝑌𝑀[𝐹𝜇𝜈]=𝑖∫𝑑4𝑥(−14𝑔2(𝐹𝜇𝜈𝑎)2)
    • We would like to discretize this

  • At small 𝑎,

    𝑊𝜇𝜈(𝑁)=𝕀+𝑖𝑎2𝐹𝜇𝜈(𝑁)−𝑎42𝐹𝜇𝜈2(𝑁)+𝑂(𝑎6)

    𝐶(𝑥)⟨Ω|𝒪︀(0)𝒪︀(𝑥)|Ω⟩=∫𝒟︀𝐴𝜇𝒟︀𝑢‾𝒟︀𝑢 𝑒𝑖𝑆𝒪︀(0)𝒪︀(𝑥)

    However, it would give a rapid phase shift. Instead, you must perform a wick rotation

9.5 Helicity Spinors

Summary:

  • Helicity spinors are a way to write polarizations 𝜀𝜇 and momentum 𝑝𝜇 in terms of a more natural way (bispinors)

    • This is more convenient specifically for calculating gluon scattering

  • They are written in the weyl representation where 𝜓𝛼 and 𝜒̃𝛼̇ are left and right handed spinors

  • Notice that spin 1 fields transform in the (12,12) representation of the Lorentz group

    • This entails that we can write them as bispinors instead of 4-vectors

  • Remember the mathematical relations for spinors in the weyl representation:

    • 𝜀𝛼𝛽𝜓𝛼(𝑥)𝜓𝛽(𝑥) and 𝜀𝛼̇𝛽̇𝜓̃𝛼̇𝜓̃𝛽̇ are L.I.

  • Some useful relations with these (and the pauli matrices) are

    𝑔𝜇𝜈𝜎𝜇𝛼𝛼̇𝜎𝜈𝛽𝛽̇=2𝜖𝛼𝛽𝜖𝛼̇𝛽̇𝜖𝛼𝛽𝜖𝛼̇𝛽̇𝜎𝜇𝛽̇𝛽=𝜎̄𝛼̇𝛼𝜇

  • For the inner product, defined as 𝜓𝜒≡𝜀𝛼𝛽𝜓𝛼(𝑥)𝜒𝛽(𝑥)

    • 𝜓𝜒=𝜒𝜓

  • All of these spinors are fields. What happens when we use constant spinors?

Definition 9.5.1 (Helicity Spinor).

  • ℝ or ℂ doublets that transform in the (12,0) or (0,12) representation of the Lorentz Group
  • The inner products for these are
  • ⟨𝜆𝜒⟩=𝜖𝛼𝛽𝜆𝛼𝜒𝛽=𝜆𝛼𝜒𝛼=−𝜆𝛼𝜒𝛼
  • [𝜆𝜒]=𝜖𝛼𝛽𝜆̃𝛼𝜒̃𝛽=𝜆̃𝛼𝜒̃𝛼=−𝜒̃𝛼𝜆̃𝛼

  • These products have some identities due to them commuting:

    ⟨𝜆𝜒⟩=−⟨𝜒𝜆⟩,[𝜆𝜒]=−[𝜒𝜆][𝜆𝜆]=⟨𝜆𝜆⟩=0

9.5.1 Momentum

  • For bispinor representation of momentum, we have:
𝑝𝛼𝛼̇≡𝜎𝛼𝛼̇𝜇𝑝𝜇=(𝑝0−𝑝3−𝑝1+𝑖𝑝2−𝑝1−𝑖𝑝2𝑝0+𝑝3)

𝜆𝛼=𝑧𝑝0−𝑝3(𝑝0−𝑝3−𝑝1−𝑖𝑝2),𝜆̃𝛼̇=𝑧1𝑝0−𝑝3(𝑝0−𝑝3,−𝑝1+𝑖𝑝2)

9.5.2 Polarizations

  • All polarizations satisfy the relation that
